transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-04-14 12:21 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-04-14T12:21:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 34.122 degrees and its azimuth is 159.921 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 18.176 degrees and its azimuth is 200.971 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 11.39 percent illuminated, 39.356 degrees from the Sun, and 375827.9 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not reliably with the unaided eye, despite it being geometrically above the horizon.

The Moon is only about 11% illuminated and just 39° from the Sun, while the Sun is high in a bright, clear daytime sky. A thin crescent can sometimes be seen in daylight, but it is usually much easier when it is farther from the Sun, higher contrast against a darker sky, or when you already have a very precise reference point.

Here the Moon is reasonably high at 18°, but it is in the same general southern sky as the Sun and only about 41° farther west in azimuth. With normal unaided vision, you might catch it if you know exactly where to search and can block the Sun safely behind a building, pole, or your hand—without ever looking toward the Sun directly—but I would not count on it.

Binoculars could make it much easier, but **do not use them anywhere near the Sun or sweep around blindly**: accidental solar viewing can cause permanent eye damage.
